1.note: The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language.

1.q: לָ⁠מָ֣ה אֱ֭לֹהִים זָנַ֣חְתָּ לָ⁠נֶ֑צַח יֶעְשַׁ֥ן אַ֝פְּ⁠ךָ֗ בְּ⁠צֹ֣אן מַרְעִיתֶֽ⁠ךָ
1.note: Asaph is using the question form to express his anguish at God’s anger toward his people. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [God, you have rejected us forever! Your nose should not smoke against the flock of your pasture.]

Asaph is using **does your nose smoke** as a common expression of the culture to mean that God is angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Why are you angry]

Here Asaph is speaking of God’s people as if they were **the flock** of a shepherd, and of God as if he were a shepherd who cares for them in **your pasture**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [against the people you care for]

Asaph is using the possessive form to describe a **flock** that is associated with a **pasture**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express the idea in another way. Alternate translation: [against the flock that you pasture]

2.note: This is an imperative, but it communicates a polite request rather than a command. See the Introduction to this Psalm for more information on how to translate the imperative here and throughout this Psalm. Alternate translation: [Please remember your congregation]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean that the tribe itself is what God inherited. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the tribe that is your inheritance]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **inheritance**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the tribe that you inherited] or [the people whom you have made your own]

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that a sentence in many languages would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if this would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [remember this Mount Zion on which you have dwelt]

3.note: The psalmist speaks of God as if he were a person with **feet** which he could **Lift up** and come and see the ruined temple in Jerusalem. The phrase **Lift up your feet** is probably also indicating that the psalmist wants God to not only take notice but also to take notice quickly. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Come and see the perpetual ruins] or [Please do not delay any longer. Please pay attention to these perpetual ruins]

Here and other places in this psalm, **the holy place** refers to the Temple in Jerusalem that had been destroyed. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could indicate that explicitly as modeled by the UST.

4.note: Here Asaph is speaking of the **adversaries** as if they were wild animals that **roared**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Your adversaries shouted loudly]

Setting up **signs** was a symbolic action by which the conquerors signified their victory over those conquered. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. The phrase **they have set up their signs as signs** could mean: (1) that God’s adversaries had set up their military banners as signs in the Temple. Alternate translation: [they have set up their banners as signs] or [they have set up their banners as a sign of their conquest] or (2) that God’s adversaries had set up items of worship and symbols related to their false religion. Alternate translation: [they have set up symbols and items for their pagan worship] or [they have set up idolatrous symbols and items of false worship]

5.note: The expression **It was known** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [They appeared]

The point of this comparison is that just as a woodsman swings **axes** to cut down trees **in a thicket**, so the enemies swung their weapons to destroy the carvings of the temple. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like a woodsman chopping down trees in a forest]

6.note: Here the words **And now** mark a shift from describing what the enemies did in the past to what they are doing in the present. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Now]
The pronoun **its** refers to the holy place. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the carvings of the holy place]

7.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. For more information on translating parallelisms, see the Introduction to this Psalm. Alternate translation: [They completely burned down and desecrated the place where you dwell]
The pronoun **They** refers to the enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The enemies sent]

Asaph is using the term **name** to represent God’s presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the place called by your name by bringing it] or [the dwelling where you are present by bringing it]

Asaph is using the possessive form to describe a **dwelling** that is characterized by God’s **name**, that is, by his presence. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express the idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the dwelling place dedicated to you by burning it]

8.note: The phrase **They said in their heart** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. Alternate translation: [They thought to themselves]
Both occurrences of the pronoun **They** refer to the enemies. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The enemies said in their heart]

Asaph is using **in their heart** as a common expression of the culture to mean that the enemies thought this to themselves. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [within themselves]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the places that are dedicated to **God** for worship. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the places where people gather to worship God]

9.note: Here the phrase **our signs** could refer to: (1) signs that God’s prophets gave. Alternate translation: [We do not see any prophetic signs for us] or [We do not see any signs given to us from a prophet] or (2) the military banners and symbols used by the Israelite army which represented their army. Alternate translation: [We no longer see any of our military banners] or (3) the Jewish festivals and religious observances which were the outward signs of their religion. Alternate translation: [We no longer see any signs of our religion] or [All our sacred observances are gone] or [All our sacred symbols are gone]

10.q: עַד־מָתַ֣י אֱ֭לֹהִים יְחָ֣רֶף צָ֑ר יְנָ֘אֵ֤ץ אוֹיֵ֖ב שִׁמְ⁠ךָ֣ לָ⁠נֶֽצַח
10.note: Asaph is using the question form to express his impatient plea for God to intervene. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate these questions as statements or exclamations. Alternate translation: [God, the adversary has reproached you long enough! The enemy should not despise your name forever.]

Asaph is using the term **name** to represent God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your reputation]

11.note: Asaph is using the question form to protest God’s inaction. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You should not hold back your hand, even your right hand!]

Asaph is using **hold back your hand** as a common expression of the culture to mean that God is withholding his action and not intervening. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [do you refrain from acting with your great power]

Here, **your hand, even your right hand** represents God’s power to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your power, even your great strength]

Here, **your bosom** represents concealment and inaction, as though God were keeping his hand tucked inside his robe instead of stretching it out to act. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [your hiding place]

12.note: Asaph uses the word **But** here to indicate a contrast between the despair he has expressed about the destruction of the temple and his confidence in God as king. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Yet God is my king]
Asaph uses the pronoun **my** instead of “our” to express a personal declaration of trust. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [is my king whom I trust]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **salvations**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [mighty things to save his people]

13.note: Asaph is stating the pronoun **You** separately, even though the verb translated as **you divided** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that it was God himself who performed this mighty act. If it would be natural in your language to use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation, or you could express this emphasis in a different way. See how you as a team decide to translate this phrase and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [It was you who divided]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you are strong]

Here Asaph is speaking of the forces of chaos as if they were **sea monsters** whose **heads** God crushed. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the powers of the chaotic waters]

14.note: Here Asaph is speaking of the forces of chaos as if they were a great sea creature called **Leviathan**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the great chaos creature]

Here Asaph is speaking of God’s defeat of Leviathan as if God had given **him as food** to people, meaning that God completely destroyed this power. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you left his remains for the people]

15.note: Here, **split open spring and wadi** refers to Yahweh breaking open the ground and causing springs and streams to flow. Alternate translation: [you caused springs and streams to flow out of the ground]

16.note: Asaph is referring to all of time by naming two extremes, **the day** and **the night**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [All hours of the day and night are also]

Here the word **also** connects two parallel statements, emphasizing that both the day and the night belong to God. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [even]

Asaph is referring to all celestial light by naming two components, **the light and the sun**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [every source of light in the sky]

17.note: Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the boundaries that mark the extent of **the earth**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the boundaries that define the earth]

Asaph is referring to all the seasons of the year by naming two extremes, **summer and winter**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the seasons of the year]

18.note: Here the words **Remember this** mark a shift from praising God’s mighty acts back to petitioning him for help. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Consider this]

Even though Asaph is addressing God directly, he is speaking of him in the third person as **Yahweh** to show respect. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [the enemy has reproached you, Yahweh]

Asaph is using the term **name** to represent God’s reputation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [has despised your reputation]

19.note: Asaph is using the possessive form to describe the **life** that belongs to the people he calls a **dove**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express the idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the lives of your people whom you cherish]

Here Asaph is speaking of God’s people as if they were a vulnerable **dove**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [your defenseless people]

Here Asaph is speaking of the enemy nation as if it were a wild **beast** that would devour its prey. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the cruel enemy]

Asaph is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [your poor people]

20.note: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because violent places fill the dark places of the land]

Asaph is using the possessive form to describe **pastures** that are characterized by **violence**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this purpose, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [violent places]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **violence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [violent deeds]

Here Asaph is speaking of places of oppression and danger as if they were **dark places**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the dangerous places of the land]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the places in **the land** that are dark, that is, dangerous. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the dark places that are in the land]

21.note: Asaph is using the adjective **weak** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the weak person]

The expression **ashamed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [feeling shame]

Asaph is using the adjectives **poor** and **needy** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [those who are poor and needy]

22.note: Here the words **Arise, God** mark a shift to a final urgent appeal for God to act. If the connection between this statement and the previous one is not clear, you may want to use a different connecting word to show how this statement relates to what comes before it. Alternate translation: [Take action, God]

Here Asaph is speaking of God as if he were a litigant who would **plead** a legal **case** in court. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Contend for yourself]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the case that is brought against God, that is, the insults directed at him. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the case against you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **reproach**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how the fool reproaches you]
Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the reproach that comes from **the fool**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the way the fool reproaches you]

23.note: Here, **the voice of your adversaries** represents what the adversaries are saying. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the words of your adversaries]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the voice that comes from **your adversaries**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [what your adversaries are saying]

Asaph is using this possessive form to mean the uproar that comes from **the ones rising against** God. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the noise that your opponents make]
